tools.name: teamup_get_calendar
tools.description: The calendar this connection points at: title, timezone and date settings, custom event fields, sub-calendars, the permission of the calendar key in use and the plan's features. Call this first to learn the sub-calendar ids and the timezone. The calendar key itself is never returned. GET /{calendarK

tools.name: teamup_list_subcalendars
tools.description: List the sub-calendars (the colored lanes that events belong to, such as people, rooms or resources). A key with admin permission also sees inactive ones. GET /{calendarKey}/subcalendars.

tools.name: teamup_get_subcalendar
tools.description: One sub-calendar by id: name, color, overlap rule, active state and which links may use it. GET /{calendarKey}/subcalendars/{id}.

tools.name: teamup_list_access_keys
tools.description: List the calendar's access keys (sharing links and user accesses) with name, role, active state and per-sub-calendar permission. Needs a key with admin permission. The secret key values are never returned (they are secrets); use the id and name to tell links apart. GET /{calendarKey}/keys.

tools.name: teamup_list_events
tools.description: List the events in a date range, optionally only on some sub-calendars. Recurring events are expanded: every occurrence in the range is returned with its own id (series id + -rid- + start). Notes come as markdown. Times use the calendar's timezone unless tz is set. GET /{calendarKey}/events.

tools.name: teamup_search_events
tools.description: Search events by keyword (2-100 characters) within a date range (default: today only, so always pass the range you mean). Recurring events are expanded. Paged with limit and offset. GET /{calendarKey}/events?query=.

tools.name: teamup_get_event
tools.description: One event by id: title, times, sub-calendars, location, who, notes (markdown), recurrence rule, custom fields, signups, comments, attachments (metadata), version, change history and reminders. Use the occurrence id (123-rid-<unix start>) for one occurrence of a recurring event. GET /{calendarKey}/ev

tools.name: teamup_list_changed_events
tools.description: Events created, changed or deleted since a Unix timestamp (at most 30 days back), for syncing. A recurring event comes back once, as its series, not as occurrences. Deleted events carry delete_dt. Pass the reply's timestamp as since_timestamp next time so nothing is missed. GET /{calendarKey}/events

tools.name: teamup_list_event_signups
tools.description: The people signed up for an event (name, email, id). Signups must be enabled on the event. GET /{calendarKey}/events/{id}/signups.

tools.name: teamup_create_event
tools.description: WRITE: create an event. Needs a calendar key with add or modify permission. Give at least subcalendar_ids, start and end. Not idempotent: a repeated call creates a second event. The reply holds the new event and an undo_id; teamup_undo_event_action removes the event again within one hour. POST /{cal

tools.name: teamup_update_event
tools.description: WRITE: change fields of an event; fields you leave out keep their value (the event is read first and sent back with its version, so a concurrent edit is refused instead of overwritten; an event without a version is not changed). Needs modify permission. For a recurring event pass redit; use the occu

tools.name: teamup_delete_event
tools.description: WRITE, DESTRUCTIVE: delete an event, or for a recurring event the chosen occurrences. Needs modify permission. Not retried. The reply holds an undo_id; teamup_undo_event_action restores the event within one hour, after that the deletion is permanent. For one occurrence use the occurrence id (123-rid

tools.name: teamup_undo_event_action
tools.description: WRITE: undo a recent event creation, update or deletion with the undo_id from that call. Works for one hour only and is refused if someone else changed the event since. PUT /{calendarKey}/events/undo/{undo_id}.

tools.name: teamup_create_subcalendar
tools.description: WRITE: create a sub-calendar. Needs a calendar key with admin permission, and the plan may limit how many exist. Not idempotent: a repeated call creates a second one. POST /{calendarKey}/subcalendars.

tools.name: teamup_update_subcalendar
tools.description: WRITE: change a sub-calendar's name, color, overlap rule or active state; fields you leave out keep their value. Needs admin permission. Making a sub-calendar inactive hides it from users without admin rights. PATCH /{calendarKey}/subcalendars/{id}.

findings.title: Description references secrets/credentials
findings.detail: Description of "teamup_list_access_keys" references sensitive artifacts (secret). A tool description has no reason to mention credentials.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta: untrusted input + private data + external sink
findings.detail: Server "mcp" exposes tools that together enable an exfiltration flow. Untrusted content: teamup_get_event, teamup_list_event_signups · Private data: teamup_list_access_keys · Public sink: teamup_list_event_signups, teamup_create_event, teamup_create_subcalendar · Destructive: teamup_create_event, teamup_update_event, teamup_delete_event.

evidence.snippet: Untrusted content: teamup_get_event, teamup_list_event_signups · Private data: teamup_list_access_keys · Public sink: teamup_list_event_signups, teamup_create_event, teamup_create_subcalendar · Destructive: teamup_create_event, teamup_update_event, teamup_delete_event

findings.remediation: Do not co-install these capabilities under one trust boundary; an injected comment/email can steer the model to exfiltrate via the sink tool.
